source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: The LLM translates the problem into a formal language (first-order logic, logic programming, constraints or SAT). A symbolic solver then does the reasoning. This beat standard and chain-of-thought prompting on all five datasets with GPT-3.5 (gpt-3.5-turbo).
numbers: Accuracy standard/CoT/Logic-LM, ChatGPT: PrOntoQA 47.40/67.80/61.00; ProofWriter 35.50/49.17/58.33; FOLIO 45.09/57.35/62.74; LogicalDeduction 40.00/42.33/65.67; AR-LSAT 20.34/17.31/26.41. GPT-4: ProofWriter 52.67/68.11/79.66; FOLIO 69.11/70.58/78.92; LogicalDeduction 71.33/75.25/87.63; AR-LSAT 33.33/35.06/43.04. Average gain +39.2 over standard and +18.4 over CoT (GPT-3.5).
limits: Temperature 0, multiple-choice format, fallback to CoT when the solver code does not run. Several benchmarks are synthetic. Self-refinement not included in this table. ChatGPT PrOntoQA: CoT 67.80 beat Logic-LM 61.00.
agent_relevance: Direct support for S2 Represent: put the rules in a checkable formal form and let code run the inference. Gains are largest on deep, multi-step problems.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: Counterexample: with GPT-4 on PrOntoQA, plain chain-of-thought beat Logic-LM. The formal route is not always better.
numbers: PrOntoQA GPT-4: standard 77.40, CoT 98.79, Logic-LM 83.20. text-davinci-003 PrOntoQA: CoT 83.00, Logic-LM 85.00.
limits: PrOntoQA is synthetic and easy for a strong model to reason about in text. Logic-LM accuracy on executable items stayed at 83.2 for GPT-4 even with 100% executable code.
agent_relevance: The formal route should be gated: use it where text reasoning is weak (deep chains, constraints), not by default. Matches guardrail G1 (act on a signal).

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: The weak link is translation, not solving. Syntax is near-perfect on synthetic data and poor on real expert-written problems.
numbers: Executable rate before self-refinement, GPT-4: PrOntoQA 100%, ProofWriter 99.0%, LogicalDeduction 100%, FOLIO 79.9%, AR-LSAT 32.6%. GPT-3.5: FOLIO 66.7%, AR-LSAT 11.3%. Accuracy when executable (GPT-4): AR-LSAT 60.0, FOLIO 80.4.
limits: Accuracy on executable items only, so biased upward. Tested at temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Represent (S2) must check that the formal version actually runs and still says what the text says. A run-check alone is not a meaning-check.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: Reasoning depth: accuracy of text methods falls with proof depth, Logic-LM much less so, because the solver carries the depth.
numbers: ProofWriter, 300 examples per depth subset (0, <=1, <=2, <=3, <=5 hops): Logic-LM minus CoT = +7.1, +5.0, +12.7, +20.0 and +39.4 points as depth rises.
limits: The paper's text labels the subsets depth-0,1,2,4,5 in one place and 0,<=1,<=2,<=3,<=5 in another. Synthetic data.
agent_relevance: A reason to move any multi-hop rule application out of the model and into a rule engine.

source: Pan et al. (2023) Logic-LM: Empowering LLMs with symbolic solvers for faithful logical reasoning
finding: Self-refinement with solver error messages fixes un-runnable code but does not fix wrong meaning. Accuracy plateaus while the executable rate keeps rising.
numbers: Executable rate gain averages +5.01 points. FOLIO GPT-4 exe rate 79.9 -> 85.8 with refinement while accuracy on executable items 80.4 -> 79.9. Accuracy stagnates after round 1-2 on FOLIO.
limits: Feedback is only the solver error text. Authors say it carries no semantic signal.
agent_relevance: Matches G2/G3: revise from real output, but a pass on syntax is not proof of faithfulness. Semantic check needs held-out cases or round-trip paraphrase.

source: Kirtania et al. (2024) Logic-LM++: Multi-step refinement for symbolic formulations
finding: Adds a pairwise LLM comparison of each proposed refinement against the previous formulation; only accepts the edit if it is judged semantically better. Small gain over Logic-LM, mostly on FOLIO and AR-LSAT with GPT-4.
numbers: Standard/CoT/Logic-LM/Logic-LM++ (column pairing GPT-3.5 then GPT-4): GPT-3.5 FOLIO 45.09/57.35/62.80/62.25, ProofWriter 35.50/49.17/58.33/58.83, AR-LSAT 20.34/17.31/26.41/28.13. GPT-4 FOLIO 69.11/70.58/78.92/84.80, ProofWriter 52.67/68.11/79.66/79.66, AR-LSAT 33.33/35.06/43.04/46.32. Claimed avg +5% over Logic-LM.
limits: No gain on ProofWriter with GPT-4; GPT-3.5 FOLIO slightly lower. Uses an LLM judge, which conflicts with G5 unless the judge sees no authorship. Observed failure: refinement turned 'No young person teaches' into 'All young people teach'.
agent_relevance: Shows the typical repair failure: fixing syntax introduces a semantic flip. A code-checked negation and quantifier test would be safer than an LLM judge.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM: Satisfiability-aided language models using declarative prompting
finding: The LLM writes a declarative spec (constraints) and a SAT/SMT solver finds the answer, instead of writing an imperative program. Beats program-aided LMs on constraint problems and sets a new best on LSAT and BoardgameQA.
numbers: Abstract: +23% over program-aided LM on a hard GSM subset (GSM-SYS). code-davinci-002 greedy, STANDARD vs COT: GSM-SYS 21.0/46.5, GSM 22.2/62.7, ALGEBRA 45.9/53.6, LSAT 22.0/23.5, BoardgameQA 44.6/60.7, CLUTRR 41.2/40.8, ProofWriter 76.6/80.1. Eight datasets in all.
limits: On plain GSM it is only on par with program-aided LM. Prior best fine-tuned results were surpassed without task training data.
agent_relevance: Declarative rules beat step-by-step code when the problem needs search. This is the reason to prefer rule form over procedure in S2.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM
finding: A solver gives three extra signals beyond a crash: UNSAT (rules conflict), AMBIG (several answers fit) and ERROR. These let the system abstain when the spec is wrong.
numbers: Table 5 correct/incorrect (ProgLM vs SatLM): GSM-SYS correct 43.3 vs 69.4, incorrect 52.5 vs 20.6. CLUTRR correct 58.9 vs 68.3, incorrect 21.0 vs 7.7, with UNSAT 20.1 vs 3.5 and AMBIG 15.5 for SatLM. GSM correct 72.7 vs 71.8.
limits: SatLM answers fewer questions than the imperative baseline; the gain is in selective accuracy. Table was partly garbled in text extraction; column order inferred from the caption.
agent_relevance: UNSAT and AMBIG are free, code-made doubt signals for G1: a 'no unique model' result is a reason to revisit the representation, not a vote.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SatLM
finding: Ablation: the gain comes from the solver, not only from the declarative format. Asking for the formal spec but answering without the solver gives about standard-prompt accuracy.
numbers: SATNOSOLVER roughly equal to STANDARD. When the solver is replaced by CoT, errors are planning errors 72.5% (GSM-SYS), 42.5% (GSM), 47.5% (CLUTRR) and execution errors 27.5%, 57.5%, 52.5%.
limits: Error split from a small manual analysis.
agent_relevance: Writing rules is not enough: the rules must be executed by code. Same lesson as LINC's Scratchpad baseline.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC: A neurosymbolic approach for logical reasoning by combining LMs with first-order logic provers
finding: The LLM only translates premises and conclusion into first-order logic; Prover9 decides. Big gain on ProofWriter for all three models, gain on FOLIO for the two smaller ones, and a loss for GPT-4 on FOLIO.
numbers: 10-way majority vote, T=0.8. FOLIO: StarCoder+ LINC 56.0 vs CoT 41.8; GPT-3.5 62.6 vs 54.9; GPT-4 LINC 72.5 vs CoT 75.3. ProofWriter (balanced subset): GPT-3.5 LINC 96.4, GPT-4 LINC 98.3; StarCoder+ with LINC beats GPT-3.5 CoT by 38 points and GPT-4 CoT by 10. Scratchpad (formulae written, no solver) did not beat the naive baseline.
limits: ProofWriter is synthetic with short sentences. Balanced subset of 360 items. For StarCoder+ and GPT-3.5, naive and scratchpad baselines were near the majority-label rate on FOLIO.
agent_relevance: A weak or small model with a prover can beat a strong model without one on rule-heavy items. The prover, not the written formulae, supplies the benefit.

source: Olausson et al. (2023) LINC
finding: Error analysis on FOLIO with GPT-4: LINC and chain-of-thought fail in different ways, so they are complementary. LINC loses information when translating (lumped symbols, missing implicit facts such as Person(Harry)); CoT states a conclusion that contradicts its own reasoning or makes an invalid step.
numbers: Syntactically invalid FOL: 38% StarCoder+, 24% GPT-3.5, 13% GPT-4. Most common syntax error: one symbol used with different arities. GPT-4 FOLIO accuracy 75.3% CoT vs 72.5% LINC with different wrong-answer sets.
limits: FOLIO annotation noise also noted. Analysis on one dataset and one model.
agent_relevance: Two independent routes (text and formal) disagree on different items. Use disagreement as the signal in G1, and keep them as different kinds of check (G4).

source: Lyu et al. (2023) Faithful Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Two stages: the LM writes a symbolic reasoning chain (Python, Datalog, PDDL) and a deterministic solver gets the answer. The chain is then a faithful explanation by construction, and accuracy mostly rose.
numbers: code-davinci-002; better than CoT on 9 of 10 datasets across 4 domains. Relative gains: math word problems +6.3%, planning +3.4%, multi-hop QA +5.5%, relational inference (CLUTRR) +21.4% (greedy). Datalog used for StrategyQA and CLUTRR, PDDL for SayCan.
limits: On StrategyQA the gain is small because difficulty is knowledge retrieval, not reasoning; authors cite subquestion errors (17%), retrieval errors (10%) and wrong reasoning from knowledge (10%). Codex model, not chat models.
agent_relevance: Datalog as the rule form for relational questions is validated; rule form helps least when the missing piece is facts, not inference.

source: Ishay, Yang, Lee (2023) Leveraging large language models to generate answer set programs
finding: Step-by-step prompting (extract constants, paraphrase clues, generate rules) lets GPT-3/GPT-4 write answer set programs for logic puzzles. Far better than asking the model to solve the puzzle directly.
numbers: Accuracy on 50 train and 100 test puzzles (Mitra and Baral set): zero-shot GPT-3 0%/2%; few-shot GPT-3 4%/3%; zero-shot GPT-4 12%/21%; few-shot GPT-4 6%/7%; GPT-3 generated ASP 86%/81%; GPT-4 generated ASP 92%/92%. Prior special-purpose system 71% test. GPT-4 test mistakes: 3 in constraint semantics versus 13 for GPT-3 in the syntax step.
limits: One puzzle type; errors are mostly simple and human-correctable per the authors. GPT-3 text-davinci-003 and GPT-4 of early 2023.
agent_relevance: Decomposing the translation into small checkable steps (constants first, then each clue) is a concrete way to build S2 reliably.

source: Yang, Ishay, Lee (2023) Coupling large language models with logic programming for robust and general reasoning from text
finding: GPT-3 turns sentences into atomic facts; reusable hand-written ASP knowledge modules do the reasoning. No retraining, a few examples per task. Strong on bAbI, StepGame, CLUTRR, gSCAN and robot planning.
numbers: bAbI average: few-shot GPT-3 80.34, CoT 86.18, GPT-3+ASP 99.99. CLUTRR 1.3 (400 items): 363 correct; 16 wrong due to dataset label mistakes, 21 due to GPT-3 parsing mistakes. Test accuracy on CLUTRR 1.3 categories (clean/supporting/irrelevant/disconnected): 97.0/84.0/92.0/90.0.
limits: Hand-written knowledge modules are needed per domain. Because the pipeline is interpretable, the authors found label errors in the original datasets.
agent_relevance: Reusable rule modules (kept across tasks) fit a library of checkable rules. Transparent rules also let the agent audit the benchmark or its own facts.

source: Borazjanizadeh and Piantadosi (2024) Reliable reasoning beyond natural language
finding: The model writes Prolog (facts, equalities, constraints) and Prolog solves. On a new 55-problem Non-Linear Reasoning set (iterative updates, backtracking, parallel chains), text-only GPT-4 fails and the Prolog route nearly solves it.
numbers: GPT-4 text-only vs Prolog: constraint satisfaction 8% -> 100%; math word problems with interdependent variables to 100%; algorithmic games 8.3% -> 66.7%. As interdependence rises from 1 to 4 variables, text-only GPT-4 falls from 100% to 0%; Prolog stays at ceiling. BIG-bench Navigate: all three models above 98% with Prolog.
limits: Hand-designed small set of 55 problems. GPT-4 was likely trained on GSM8k, so GSM8k gains are smaller for it. Five-shot prompts per category. GPT-3.5 only encoded constraints correctly about half the time.
agent_relevance: Best evidence that failures from tracking many linked variables vanish when the state lives in a logic program. Strong case for S2 plus a code-run check.

source: Wang et al. (2024) ChatLogic: Integrating logic programming with large language models for multi-step reasoning
finding: LLM translates the question into logic code run by an inference engine, with syntax and semantic correction modules. Helps weak models most; GPT-4 with zero-shot CoT is sometimes equal or better.
numbers: PARARULE-Plus total accuracy (100 samples): GPT-3.5 Base 0.344, zero-shot CoT 0.3875, ChatLogic 0.5275; GPT-4 Base 0.555, CoT 0.69, ChatLogic 0.73; Llama 2-7B Base 0.0475, CoT 0.105, ChatLogic 0.1825. Row-to-model pairing inferred from the table layout.
limits: Small samples (100 per set); on CONCEPTRULES zero-shot CoT matched or beat it for GPT-4. Generated code judged executable by absence of error messages only.
agent_relevance: Gains shrink as the base model gets stronger. Keep the formal route for hard depth, not as a fixed rule.

source: Saparov and He (2023) Language models are greedy reasoners: a systematic formal analysis of chain-of-thought
finding: PrOntoQA parses CoT into symbolic proofs. InstructGPT and GPT-3 take correct single deduction steps even in fictional worlds. Their weakness is proof planning: when several valid steps exist, they do not explore systematically.
numbers: Label accuracy tracks lenient proof-accuracy measures (skip and valid proofs) better than strict proof accuracy. Paper points to neurosymbolic search as the fix.
limits: Per-condition numbers are in figures that I could not read from the extracted text; only the qualitative result is recorded. GPT-3-era models.
agent_relevance: The model is a good rule applier but a poor planner. Let a rule engine do search and keep the model to one step at a time.

source: Clark, Tafjord, Richardson (2020) Transformers as soft reasoners over language
finding: RuleTaker: a transformer trained on synthetic facts and rules in English answers true/false under closed-world reasoning, and generalises to deeper proofs than it saw. Foundational older AI system for natural-language rule reasoning.
numbers: About 99% accuracy on held-out synthetic data; 95%+ on deeper chains (up to depth 5) than seen in training; transfers to two hand-authored rule sets and to paraphrased rule bases.
limits: Trained on synthetic rule data; closed-world assumption; transfer limited to the tested sets.
agent_relevance: Shows rules can be given in natural language and still be followed, but only inside the training distribution. Reason to prefer explicit executable rules.

source: Tafjord, Dalvi, Clark (2021) ProofWriter: generating implications, proofs, and abductive statements
finding: A generative model produces implications and proofs by repeating a one-step implication generator. Proofs reflect real model decisions, not after-the-fact stories, and generalise to unseen depths.
numbers: On the RuleTaker data proof accuracy exceeds earlier methods by +9% absolute. Abduction: can generate missing facts that make a statement provable, with high precision.
limits: Synthetic rule data; abduction tested on limited sets.
agent_relevance: Step-wise forward chaining in small checked steps is the part that works. Abduction of missing facts is a model for an operator that asks what fact is missing.

source: Sun et al. (2024) Think-on-Graph: deep and responsible reasoning of LLM on knowledge graph
finding: An LLM agent runs beam search over a knowledge graph, choosing relations and entities step by step, so the answer comes with a traceable path. No training. A small model plus ToG can beat a bigger model without the graph.
numbers: Hits@1, ToG with GPT-4 vs ChatGPT IO prompt: CWQ 67.6 vs 37.6, WebQSP 82.6 vs 63.3, GrailQA 81.4 vs 29.4, QALD10-en 53.8 vs 42.0, Simple Questions 66.7 vs 20.0. ToG-R GPT-4 CWQ 69.5. State of the art on 6 of 9 datasets. Fine-tuned best: CWQ 70.4, WebQSP 82.1, GrailQA 75.4, Simple Questions 85.8.
limits: Needs a well-formed graph (Freebase, Wikidata); many LLM calls; below fine-tuned systems on Simple Questions and CWQ.
agent_relevance: Closest published example of a knowledge-graph fact store used inside an LLM agent loop: the graph supplies facts, the model only picks the next edge.

source: Lenat and Marcus (2023) Getting from generative AI to trustworthy AI: what LLMs might learn from Cyc
finding: Argues that trustworthy AI needs a hybrid of LLMs and an explicit-knowledge system. Describes Cyc: about four decades, a 50-person project, tens of millions of hand-written axioms in CycL (higher-order logic with contexts) with default rules and step-by-step provenance. Lists 16 desiderata.
numbers: No benchmark numbers. 16 desiderata; Cyc reasons in higher-order logic in real time using specialised reasoners.
limits: A position paper by Cyc's founder; no controlled comparison with LLMs. Cost of building knowledge bases by hand is the main limit.
agent_relevance: Gives a design list for S2 rules: provenance, contexts (microtheories), default rules that can be overridden, and audit trails. Hand-built knowledge is slow; an LLM could draft, code could check.

source: Szeider (2026) ASP-Bench: from natural language to logic programs
finding: An agent loop (ReAct style) with an ASP solver tool writes, tests and fixes answer set programs. With Claude Sonnet 4.5 it solved every problem in the benchmark, every run. The benchmark has 128 problems, 64 base problems each in easy and hard form.
numbers: All runs correct: 2 runs on easy, 3 on hard. Hard problems took on average 7.7 solver-execution calls; range 3.7 (queens domination, zebra puzzle) to 26.0 (DNA sequence assembly); who-is-the-killer 20.0. Error correction was under 10% of agent steps even on the hardest. Earlier best on the NL-ASP-200 set 58.5%. Solver calls limited to 20 s.
limits: Saturated, so it no longer ranks methods. Single model, temperature 0. The project prompt was tuned for five iterations on a few easy problems first; validators are the ground truth.
agent_relevance: Direct match: model drafts, solver runs, and testing single rules takes a larger share of steps as problems get harder. Supports testing one rule at a time (G2, G3).

source: Borroto Santana et al. (2026) BLAST: benchmarking LLMs with ASP-based structured testing
finding: Eight LLMs on ten graph problems: nearly all models write ASP that parses, but few write ASP that is right. Semantic accuracy is measured with test suites and a model-based check; paraphrasing the problem also lowers it.
numbers: Models: o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 1.5 Pro, GPT-4o, GPT-5, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Llama 3.3 70B. Syntactic scores mostly 0.6 to 1.0 per problem; semantic scores in the heatmap often 0 to 0.4, best about 0.7 to 0.9 on a few problems. GPT-5 had lower syntactic scores than most.
limits: Graph problems only; numbers read from a heatmap in extracted text, so approximate. Semantic metric partly depends on GPT-4o as predicate matcher and paraphraser.
agent_relevance: Executable is not equal to correct. This is the empirical case for G3: check against held-out test cases, not the examples the code was fitted to.

source: Borroto, Kareem, Ricca (2024), as reported in ASP-Bench (2026)
finding: One-shot generation is often wrong: ChatGPT-3.5 produced flawed programs for most graph problems.
numbers: Flawed programs for 17 of 21 graph problems (as reported in ASP-Bench's introduction).
limits: Second-hand: read in ASP-Bench, not in the original paper.
agent_relevance: One-shot rule writing should not be trusted; iterate against a solver.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Can large language models understand DL-Lite ontologies? An empirical study
finding: Six tasks on description-logic ontologies. LLMs understand the formal syntax and the model-theoretic meaning of concepts and roles well, but fail on transitivity of negative inclusions and on ontologies with large ABoxes (many instance facts).
numbers: Small ontologies: near 100% on subsumption and instance checking (GPT-4o deduced all implications on the three smaller UOBM ontologies). Above a size threshold performance drops to nearly 0%. Models: GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, LLaMA3-8B; prompts with and without rules and examples. Inconsistency detection: good on economy-Inc. (29 minimal inconsistent sets), worse on Maa-edas-iasted (38 sets).
limits: DL-Lite is a light description logic. Per-cell numbers are in figures not readable from text.
agent_relevance: Facts must stay small: a large fact base in the prompt is where the model collapses. Keep big fact stores in a reasoner and pass only the relevant slice.

source: Yang, Chen, Sattler (2026) Large language model for OWL proofs
finding: Tests whether LLMs can build proofs from OWL (EL) ontologies: extract needed axioms, simplify them, explain steps, and judge whether the premises are complete. Logical complexity matters more than formal versus natural language form. Noise and missing premises hurt a lot.
numbers: Extraction falls by up to 47% with heavy irrelevant axioms and up to 38% with missing premises; simplification and derivation accuracy fall by around 47%, 42% and 53% in the noisy settings. Formal logic versus natural language form: less than 8% drop. Some 32B models score above 70% on extraction; others show large gaps. An in-context aid raised one score by up to 16-fold (3.82% to 61.95% on Snomed).
limits: EL fragment only; ontologies include GO-Plus, FoodOn and Snomed; results vary a lot between models.
agent_relevance: Give the agent complete, clean premises and ask it to flag missing premises. Irrelevant axioms cost as much as missing ones.

source: Meng et al. (2025) OntoURL: a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on symbolic ontological understanding, reasoning and learning
finding: 57,303 questions over 40 ontologies, 15 tasks, 20 open-source LLMs, zero-shot. Models are good at reading ontologies, worse at reasoning, weakest at building them.
numbers: Understanding: class relations (U2) and instance classification (U4) 80-94%. Reasoning: inferred relations (R1) 3-4 points below U2; instance class reasoning R3 60-70% vs U4 80-90%. SWRL (R4) and description logic reasoning (R5) 60-75% across models; best model Qwen2.5-72B. Learning tasks L2-L4 near 0 for most models.
limits: Open-source models only, zero-shot. Later versions of the paper changed some claims (v3 says LLMs outperform humans in understanding and reasoning).
agent_relevance: Formal-logic operators cost 10-20 points even when plain-language inference is fine. Another reason to run description-logic and rule reasoning in a reasoner.
